## 2. One model, two scales

The logistic model connects a linear predictor to a probability:

\[
\eta = \beta_0 + \beta_1x
\qquad\qquad
p = \operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta)
\]

```{r logistic-link-figure}
eta <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 300)
p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-eta))
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(p, log(p / (1 - p)), type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Probability, p", ylab = "Log odds",
     main = "Logit")
abline(h = 0, v = 0.5, lty = 3)
plot(eta, p, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Log odds, eta", ylab = "Probability, p",
     main = "Inverse-logit", ylim = c(0, 1))
abline(h = 0.5, v = 0, lty = 3)
```

**a.** The linear predictor \(\eta\) can range from \(-\infty\) to \(+\infty\). What range must \(p\) occupy?

Answer: ______________________________________________________________

**b.** What probability corresponds to \(\eta = 0\)?

Answer: ______________________________________________________________

**c.** As \(\eta\) becomes very large and positive, what happens to \(p\)? As \(\eta\) becomes very negative?

## 3. Read a logistic curve

```{r logistic-curve}
x <- seq(-4, 4, length.out = 300)
p <- 1 / (1 + exp(-x))
plot(x, p, type = "l", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Predictor, x", ylab = "Predicted probability",
     ylim = c(0, 1))
abline(h = 0.5, v = 0, lty = 3)
```

## 5. Effect size depends on where you start

Both curves below have the same slope on the logit scale (\(\beta_1=0.5\)), but different intercepts.

```{r same-slope-curves}
x <- seq(-5, 5, length.out = 300)
p1 <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(-2 + 0.5 * x)))
p2 <- 1 / (1 + exp(-(1 + 0.5 * x)))
plot(x, p1, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 1),
     xlab = "Predictor, x", ylab = "Predicted probability")
lines(x, p2, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Intercept = -2", "Intercept = 1"),
       lty = c(1, 2), bty = "n")
```

**a.** Do equal slopes on the logit scale imply equal probability differences at a given \(x\)?  
☐ Yes  ☐ No

**b.** Why is back-transforming predictions to the probability scale often useful for biological interpretation?

________________________________________________________________________

________________________________________________________________________

## 7. How well does the model discriminate?

The plots show predicted probabilities for cases actually observed as 0 or 1.

```{r discrimination-figure}
set.seed(42)
n <- 24
a0 <- runif(n, 0.10, 0.80)
a1 <- runif(n, 0.15, 0.75)
b0 <- runif(n, 0.02, 0.40)
b1 <- runif(n, 0.60, 0.98)

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(5, 4, 3, 1))
stripchart(list(a0, a1), vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 1, xaxt = "n", ylim = c(0, 1),
           xlab = "Observed outcome", ylab = "Predicted probability",
           main = "Model A")
axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Observed 0", "Observed 1"))
stripchart(list(b0, b1), vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 1, xaxt = "n", ylim = c(0, 1),
           xlab = "Observed outcome", ylab = "Predicted probability",
           main = "Model B")
axis(1, at = 1:2, labels = c("Observed 0", "Observed 1"))
```

**a.** Which model discriminates better?

Answer: ____________________
